findings.description: The EBS data volume does not set encrypted = true or a KMS key, so its contents may be stored unencrypted unless an account-level default happens to apply. The attached disk and its data could be exposed if underlying storage is accessed improperly.

The instance user-data embeds an AWS access key ID and secret access key in plaintext. User data is retrievable by principals with instance describe access and the credentials are also exposed in source control and on the instance.

No metadata_options block requires IMDSv2, leaving the instance able to use IMDSv1. An SSRF flaw in software on this host could then retrieve instance metadata credentials if an instance role is later attached.
TCP port 22 is open to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing any internet host to attempt SSH access to the publicly addressed instance. This materially expands the brute-force and exploit attack surface.
The security group permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0. A compromised portal instance can use this unrestricted egress for data exfiltration or command-and-control.
The bucket has no server-side encryption configuration, so VPC flow logs written to it are not explicitly protected with encryption at rest. These logs can contain sensitive network metadata.
The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block resource to prevent public ACLs or bucket policies. This leaves the flow-log archive susceptible to accidental or later public exposure.

The snapshot is created from an EBS volume that is not explicitly encrypted, so the resulting backup is likewise not protected by encryption at rest. Backup contents may therefore be exposed independently of the running instance.
